title: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
summary: A local account lives on one machine only and is defined in that host's own account database, so its permissions stop at that system. Organisations create them for users, remote support, services, and emergency administration, and because machines are frequently built from one image, the same local password can exist across an entire fleet. Adversaries abuse them in two ways: signing in locally after learning the password, or reusing that one password to move from host to host. A local administrator account is especially valuable because it can then dump further credentials from memory and widen access. Detection depends on correlating logon events across machines, looking for one local account authenticating to many endpoints or a local administrator logging on interactively where no maintenance is scheduled.

beginner.definition: A local account is a login that exists on one computer only. It is stored on that machine and gives access to that machine, not to the whole network. Support teams and services often use local accounts because they are simple to set up. This is a sub-technique of valid accounts, which covers the abuse of real logins.
beginner.whyItMatters: Local accounts are easy to forget about, so their passwords often stay the same for years. When many computers share one local password, one stolen secret opens all of them. Attackers use these accounts to keep access after the first password is changed. Because the login is real, no alarm about a broken door ever sounds. Only comparing activity across machines reveals the pattern.
howItWorks: A technician creates a local account on a computer for support, a service, or emergency access.
The same system image is copied to many machines, so the same local password appears everywhere.
An attacker who reads that password from one host can try it on every other host.
They log on locally or through a remote service and act with whatever rights the account holds.
A local administrator account can then read further credentials from memory to widen access.
Defenders spot it when one local account logs on to many machines in a short period.
beginner.example: Think of a block of flats where every front door uses the same simple key so the caretaker can enter any flat. The caretaker finds this convenient. A thief who copies the key once can now open every door in the building without leaving a scratch. Each flat still looks secure from the inside. Local accounts work like that shared caretaker key, and only a careful record of who entered which flat shows the abuse.
takeaways: Give each machine a different local administrator password, or manage it centrally.
Watch for one local account signing in to many computers.
Rename or disable unused local accounts and review service logins.

objectives: Explain what makes an account local rather than a domain account.
Describe how password reuse across local accounts enables lateral movement.
Explain how a local administrator account is used to harvest more credentials.
Identify log evidence that shows one local account appearing on many hosts.
Summarise the steps that reduce the value of a stolen local credential.
